summary: Presents the IPng Area Directors' recommendation on what should replace the current version of the Internet Protocol. It led to the design that became IPv6. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The leaders pick the next version of the internet's address system and explain why.

subtitle: The IPng Area Directors explain why the SIPP design, with 16-byte addresses, should become the next Internet Protocol.

tldr.problem: By 1990 projections showed that the 32-bit IPv4 address space and the backbone routing tables would become limiting. The IETF had several competing proposals for a successor and needed to pick one.
tldr.mechanism: The IPng Area Directors set technical criteria, reviewed the CATNIP, SIPP and TUBA proposals, and recommended a revised SIPP with fixed 16-byte addresses. The RFC also recommends working groups, security requirements and a transition effort.
tldr.outcome: The recommended protocol was assigned version number 6 and is called IPv6. The RFC calls its own IPv6 description an overview snapshot and points readers to the standards documents for definitive specifications.

today: RFC 1752 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the January 1995 recommendation that led to IPv6; the RFC itself says its IPv6 overview is a snapshot and defers to the standards documents.

sections.title: Why a New IP Was Needed
sections.content:
Early TCP/IP designers did not foresee the scale of today's Internet. A 1987 estimate projected a need to address as many as 100,000 networks at some vague point in the future, and the RFC says that mark would be reached by 1996. IPv4's 32-bit addresses can enumerate over 4 billion hosts on as many as 16.7 million networks, but real assignment efficiency is far lower, made worse by the coarse Class A, B and C granularity.

In August 1990 three IETF participants projected that the Class B space would be exhausted by March 1994. Handing out many Class C addresses instead made backbone routing tables grow faster. The IETF formed the Routing and Addressing (ROAD) group in November 1991, which endorsed CIDR route aggregation and a call for proposals for bigger addresses. The IETF issued that call in July 1992, after rejecting an IAB recommendation to base "IPv7" on CLNP.

The IETF formed the IPng Area in late 1993. Its Address Lifetime Expectations (ALE) working group projected that the IPv4 address space would run out between 2005 and 2011, with caveats the RFC lists. That left enough time to add features rather than only enlarge addresses. The Directors endorsed current address assignment policies, saw no need to reclaim addresses or forcibly renumber, and agreed that CIDR-style blocks out of unassigned Class A space should be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet's house numbers were being handed out too fast, and the map of routes was getting too big. Leaders decided to plan a bigger system while there was still time.

sections.title: The Technical Criteria
sections.content:
To judge proposals fairly, the Directors gathered input: a call for white papers (RFC 1550) that drew twenty one responses, a requirements BOF and mailing-list discussion. This fed a document titled "Technical Criteria for Choosing IP The Next Generation (IPng)", which became the basic guideline.

The criteria include a complete specification (select by reference to documents, not future work), architectural simplicity, scale of at least 10**9 leaf-networks, topological flexibility, performance, robust service, a straightforward transition plan from IPv4, media independence, datagram service, configuration ease with automatic configuration of hosts and routers, security, unique names, free access to the standards, multicast, extensibility without network-wide upgrades, service classes, mobility, a control protocol (such as ping and traceroute), and tunneling support.
sections.plainLanguage: Before choosing, the leaders wrote a checklist: it must be big enough, simple, safe, easy to set up, and able to grow later. Then they graded each plan against it.

sections.title: The Three Candidates
sections.content:
Many proposals had appeared since 1992. By the time of the review three remained: CATNIP (Common Architecture for the Internet), SIPP (Simple Internet Protocol Plus) and TUBA (TCP/UDP over CLNP-Addressed Networks). The IESG saw Nimrod as too much of a research project to be a candidate.

  • CATNIP was a convergence protocol meant to integrate CLNP, IP and IPX, using OSI NSAP-format addresses.
  • SIPP was an evolutionary step from IPv4, with 64-bit addresses at that stage, a new way of encoding header options and a way to label traffic flows.
  • TUBA kept TCP, UDP and existing applications but ran them over CLNP with its larger NSAP addresses.

Reviewers found problems in all three. CATNIP was not completely specified and was judged too incomplete to consider. SIPP was called an aesthetically beautiful protocol, but its IPAE transition plan was seen as fatally flawed, and most reviewers thought 64-bit addresses gave inadequate room for hierarchy. TUBA's strength was existing CLNP-capable routers, but CLNP had technical shortcomings, and the TUBA community disagreed about whether the IETF could change the CLNP standards. The RFC stresses that the summary table does not necessarily reflect the Directors' views.
sections.plainLanguage: Three plans were on the table. One was unfinished, one had a tricky switch-over plan and addresses that were too short, and one was built on an older system the group could not easily change.

sections.title: The Revised Proposal and the Recommendation
sections.content:
After a retreat on May 19th and 20th 1994, two SIPP working group co-chairs proposed changes to SIPP: change the address size from 8 bytes to 16 bytes (fixed length), allow optional serverless autoconfiguration using the IEEE 802 address as the low-order part, require higher-layer protocols that embed addresses to use the whole 16-byte address, and do not use the Routing header for extended addressing. The group then published a revised SIPP, a new addressing architecture and a simplified transition mechanism.

The RFC describes the result as a synthesis: the basic protocol from SIPP, autoconfiguration and transition influenced by TUBA, an addressing structure based on CIDR work, and a routing header evolved from SDRP. On address length, a clear majority view held that 16-byte fixed-length addresses were the best compromise between efficiency, functionality, flexibility and global applicability.

The Directors recommend that "Simple Internet Protocol Plus (SIPP) Spec. (128 bit ver)" be adopted as the basis for IPng, together with the other documents listed in Appendix C. They state their belief that it meets the criteria document. They say the base specifications are complete, though transition and address autoconfiguration remained to be finalized. The IANA assigned version number 6, so the protocol is called IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The best plan got fixes: longer house numbers of one fixed size and easier setup. Then the leaders said, let's build on this one, and it became version 6.

sections.title: The IPv6 Header
sections.content:
The RFC gives an overview of IPv6 as an evolutionary step: functions that worked in IPv4 were kept, those that did not or were rarely used were removed or made optional, and a few new features were added. Addresses grow from 32 bits to 128 bits, and a scope field is added to multicast addresses. The header was simplified: although the addresses are four times longer than IPv4's, the header is only twice the size of IPv4's.

The fixed header has a 4-bit Version (6), a 28-bit Flow Label to request special handling such as non-default quality of service, a 16-bit Payload Length, an 8-bit Next Header using the same values as the IPv4 Protocol field, an 8-bit Hop Limit, and 128-bit source and destination addresses. Each forwarding node decrements the hop limit by 1 and discards the packet if it reaches zero. If Payload Length is 0, the real length is in a Hop-by-Hop option, which allows payloads larger than 64K bytes. The RFC credits the simpler processing, aligned fields and the removal of the header checksum with enabling high performance.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 packet starts with a label that says who sent it, who it is for, how many hops it may still take, and what comes next. The labels are longer, but the label itself stays tidy.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
In IPv6, optional internet-layer information goes into separate extension headers between the IPv6 header and the transport-layer header, each identified by a distinct Next Header value. Because most are not examined by routers along the path, packets with options are cheaper to forward, and options are not limited to the 40 bytes IPv4 allows.

  • Hop-by-Hop Options (Next Header value 0) carry information every node must examine. End-to-End Options are examined only by the destination.
  • Options are Type-Length-Value encoded. The top two bits of the Option Type say what to do with an unknown option: skip it, discard the packet, or discard it and send an ICMP message to the source.
  • The Routing header lists intermediate nodes to visit, designed to support SDRP. Its source route length may not exceed 24.
  • The Fragment header (Next Header value 44) is used by the source to send payloads larger than the path MTU; unlike IPv4, only source nodes fragment, not routers.
  • The Authentication header (Next Header value 51) gives authentication and integrity. The Privacy header encrypts either a transport-layer frame or an entire IPv6 datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra instructions go in separate envelopes inside the packet. Routers can ignore most of them and just pass the packet along, so the mail still moves quickly.

sections.title: Working Groups, Transition and Impact
sections.content:
The RFC recommends an IPng Working Group (chaired by Steve Deering and Ross Callon, with Robert Hinden as editor), an IPng Reviewer to keep a consistent view across areas (Dave Clark), an Address Autoconfiguration Working Group, an IPng Transition (NGTRANS) group and the longer-term TACIT group. Autoconfiguration aims at plug and play, from an isolated network to the full facilities of DHCP.

The transition plan has four requirements: incremental upgrade, incremental deployment, easy addressing (existing IPv4 hosts keep their addresses when upgraded) and low start-up costs. Dual-stack, encapsulation and header translation mechanisms are to be defined.

The RFC also counts the impact. At least 27 of the then 51 full Internet Standards need revision, plus at least 6 of 20 Draft Standards and 25 of 130 Proposed Standards. The IPng Working Group would define new versions of ICMP, ARP/RARP and UDP. Non-IETF standards and products that depend on IPv4 address size or structure must change too, and the RFC suggests Informational RFCs on the sockets, TLI/XTI and WINSOCK interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the internet's address system is a big job. The leaders asked for teams to handle setup, the switch-over, and updating every other rule that mentions the old addresses.

sections.title: Security Recommendations
sections.content:
The Directors argue that a better basic level of security is vital to the Internet's success, and that packet-level authentication would support a widespread security infrastructure. They recommend keeping authentication and encryption separate so each can be used independently.

They recommend that IPv6 support packet authentication as a basic and required function: support for the Authentication Header and a specific authentication algorithm should be required, as should support for the Privacy Header and a specific privacy algorithm. The algorithms were to be chosen by the time the IPv6 documents became Proposed Standards. A key management infrastructure is needed but is outside the scope of the IPv6 effort. The RFC also recommends an "IPv6 framework for firewalls" and notes that the added security may cost performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone should be able to check that a message really came from who it says and, if they want, keep it secret. The plan says every IPv6 device must be able to do the checking.

viz.caption: REVIEWER VIEWS ON FOUR CRITERIA (RFC 1752 SECTION 8)
IPV6 HEADER AS DRAWN IN RFC 1752

fields.name: Flow Label
fields.desc: Labels packets needing special handling, such as non-default quality of service.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Octets after the IPv6 header; 0 means the length is in a Hop-by-Hop option.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the header that follows; same values as the IPv4 Protocol field.

fields.name: Hop Limit
fields.desc: Decremented by 1 at each forwarding node; packet discarded at zero.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: Address of the intended recipient, possibly not the ultimate one if a Routing Header is present.

viz.caption: TOP TWO BITS OF OPTION TYPE (RFC 1752 SECTION 12.2.2)

items.label: Skip
items.desc: Skip over this option and continue processing the header.

items.label: Discard and report
items.desc: Discard the packet and send an ICMP Unrecognized Type message to the packet's Source Address.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the header that follows the Fragment header.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Fragment Offset
fields.desc: Offset of the payload in 8-octet units, relative to the original payload.

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Zero on transmission; ignored on reception.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: 1 means more fragments; 0 means the last fragment.

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Identifies all fragments of the same original payload.
